newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu, Clinton to discuss stalled peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu, Clinton to discuss stalled peace talks.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu leaves on Sunday for talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton on how to revive the stalled Israeli-Palestinian peace process.
"Netanyahu is going to Washington to try to put peace talks back on track," said David Bar-Illan, the prime minister's communications director.
Clinton was expected to put Netanyahu under heavy pressure at a White House meeting on Monday to make a conciliatory gesture towards the Palestinians that would allow negotiations to resume.
The talks were halted after Israel began work last month on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, sparking daily clashes between Palestinians and Israeli troops.
Palestinian officials warned that Israeli policies were in danger of provoking an "explosion" which could lead to more confrontations.
Netanyahu begins his U.S. visit in Minnesota where he will meet Jordan's King Hussein, who is undergoing surgery there, before flying on to Washington late on Sunday.
Palestinian official Hanan Ashrawi is also going to Washington, where she was due to meet U.S. administration officials on behalf of Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
"The purpose of my visit is to meet with the American administration...and to present the Palestinian point of view in terms of settlements and Jerusalem," she told Reuters.
Thousands of Israelis attended a pro-peace rally in Tel Aviv on Saturday night and urged Netanyahu to start talks intended to decide the "final status" of Palestinian self-rule areas.
Israeli opposition leader Shimon Peres, defeated by Netanyahu in elections last May, slammed the prime minister and called for an immediate return to the negotiating table.
U.S. officials said the peace process had reached one of the most serious moments in its history but they had ideas for breaking the deadlock.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns declined to give details but he said: "We're very active. We are developing our own ideas and we're going to put them foward."
The Palestinians have said that Arafat will not negotiate with Netanyahu any longer unless Israel stops work on the new settlement -- something the Israeli leader has vowed not to do.
Israel, for its part, accuses Arafat of giving a green light for Islamic suicide bombings and as conditioned the future of talks on a Palestinian crackdown on "terrorism".
